posts.title: Your Transformer Can Hold Two Thoughts at Once
posts.subtitle: New research shows blending two prompts' embeddings gets you a superposition of both answers back
posts.summary: A September 2026 paper finds transformers behave close to linear: averaging the embeddings of two unrelated prompts produces an output that's roughly a superposition of what the model would have said to each prompt alone. The effect is architectural, fades with more pretraining, can be restored by lightweight fine-tuning, and can be exploited by a guided decoding procedure to recover two coherent answers from a single forward pass.

slides.title: One Forward Pass, Two Coherent Answers
slides.body: A September 2026 paper finds that transformers are close to linear: feed in the averaged embeddings of two unrelated prompts, and the model's output is approximately the superposition of what it would have said to each prompt separately.
bullets: Paper: "Your Transformer Can Hold Two Thoughts at Once: Evidence of Linear Superposition in LLMs" (arXiv 2609.29845)
Authors: Tikhonov, Korznikov, Mikhalchuk, Dragunov, Rahmatullaev, Druzhinina, Razzhigaev, Oseledets, Tutubalina

slides.title: Why Would a Transformer Ever Be 'Linear'?
slides.body: Deep networks are built from nonlinear pieces — attention softmax, layer norm, MLP activations — specifically so they can't be reduced to simple addition. The paper asks whether that nonlinearity actually erases linear structure in what the model computes, or just hides it.
bullets: Test: average the token embeddings of Prompt A and Prompt B position-by-position, feed the blend through the model
Naive expectation: the nonlinear layers should scramble the two signals into gibberish
What they find instead: the output next-token distribution looks like a superposition of Prompt A's distribution and Prompt B's distribution

slides.title: The Superposition Linearity Hypothesis
slides.body: The authors formalize this as the Superposition Linearity Hypothesis: across the stack of attention and MLP blocks, transformers preserve enough linear structure that combining two inputs approximately combines their outputs.
bullets: The effect isn't a training artifact bolted on for one task — it shows up as an intrinsic property of the Transformer architecture itself
It's strongest in less-trained checkpoints and fades as pretraining continues, as the model becomes more nonlinear and specialized
The structure isn't destroyed, just suppressed: lightweight fine-tuning can substantially restore it

slides.title: From a Curiosity to a Decoding Trick
slides.body: Finding superposition is one thing; using it is another. The authors build a guided decoding procedure that actively disentangles the two overlapping next-token distributions, so the model can generate two separate, coherent continuations from a single blended forward pass.
bullets: Standard decoding on a blended input just produces one muddled continuation that half-follows both prompts
Guided decoding steers the sampling process to peel apart 'thread A' and 'thread B' at each step
Net effect: one forward pass, two independent, legible outputs — instead of running the model twice

slides.title: Worked Example: Two Prompts, One Pass
slides.body: Imagine blending 'Write a haiku about autumn' with 'List three causes of the French Revolution.' A normal model given the averaged embedding would likely output a garbled non-answer to both. With the guided decoding procedure, it separates the streams enough to recover something close to a haiku on one thread and a bulleted history answer on the other — from a single set of forward-pass computations.
bullets: This isn't the model literally running twice — it's one pass whose hidden states carry both threads in superposition
The disentangling happens at decode time, not by re-running the transformer

slides.title: Standard vs. Superposition-Guided Decoding
slides.body: The appeal is throughput: if you could reliably answer two prompts per forward pass, you'd roughly halve inference cost for that workload. The catch is quality — disentangled outputs are described as coherent, not as strong as answering each prompt alone.

rows: Coherent but degraded vs. answering separately
Research finding, not a shipped feature

slides.title: Where This Breaks Down
slides.body: This is an interpretability finding, not a production inference technique yet — and it works against production trends: instruction-tuning and RLHF, the very steps that make chat models useful, are exactly what suppresses the linear superposition the technique needs.
bullets: Heavily fine-tuned/RLHF'd chat models show weaker superposition than earlier-pretraining checkpoints — you may need extra fine-tuning just to restore the property
Blending unrelated prompts risks cross-talk: without the guided decoding step, outputs blur into an unusable mix
No evidence yet that this holds at every model scale or preserves quality parity with independent decoding — an early research signal, not a deployable 2x speedup

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Transformers carry more linear structure than their nonlinear building blocks would suggest — averaging two inputs approximately averages their outputs
This linearity is architectural, appears early in training, and is actively suppressed (not erased) as pretraining and fine-tuning proceed
A guided decoding procedure can exploit the residual linear structure to recover two separate answers from one forward pass
It's a mechanistic-interpretability result with a tantalizing efficiency angle — worth watching, not yet something to deploy

questions.prompt: What is the "Superposition Linearity Hypothesis" the paper proposes?
options: Transformers randomly forget half of any blended input
Combining two inputs' embeddings approximately combines (superposes) their separate outputs
Transformers can only process one prompt per forward pass
Attention layers are literally linear functions with no nonlinearity
questions.explanation: The hypothesis says the model's output for a linear combination of two inputs looks like the corresponding combination of the two individual outputs — evidence that transformers behave more linearly than their nonlinear components would suggest.

questions.prompt: According to the paper, what happens to the superposition effect as pretraining continues?
options: It strengthens monotonically
It stays constant regardless of training
It diminishes as pretraining progresses
It only appears after RLHF
questions.explanation: The authors found the effect is strongest early on and fades with more pretraining, suggesting the model becomes more specialized and nonlinear over time — though lightweight fine-tuning can restore it.

questions.prompt: What does the paper's guided decoding procedure actually do?
options: Runs the model twice, once per prompt
Disentangles a blended forward pass's output into two separate coherent continuations
Deletes one of the two blended prompts before decoding
Increases the model's context window
questions.explanation: Rather than re-running the transformer per prompt, the guided decoding procedure steers sampling to peel apart the superposed next-token distributions into two separate, legible outputs from a single forward pass.

references.title: Your Transformer Can Hold Two Thoughts at Once: Evidence of Linear Superposition in LLMs (arXiv:2609.29845)

posts.title: Anthropic's 8-Month Hunt for Misused Claude
posts.subtitle: Inside the September 2026 threat intelligence report: espionage, fraud, and fake news networks — all disrupted
posts.summary: Anthropic's September 2026 threat intelligence report details real operations disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026 — Russian-nexus espionage, a terabyte-scale cybercrime ring, autonomous zero-day research, and election-targeted influence campaigns — across seven harm areas, using Claude Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus.

slides.title: Anthropic's 8-Month Hunt for Misused Claude
slides.body: In its September 2026 threat intelligence report, Anthropic detailed operations it disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026 — spanning cyber espionage, fraud, and influence campaigns run with the help of Claude.
bullets: Report covers seven harm areas: cyber operations, influence operations, surveillance, scams & fraud, biological misuse, conventional weapons development, and illicit model distillation
Threat actors ranged from state-sponsored groups to financially motivated criminals, spyware vendors, and propaganda operations

slides.title: The Same Capabilities That Help Also Attack
slides.body: An AI that can automate coding, research, and content generation for legitimate users can automate the same tasks for espionage, fraud, and propaganda — the report exists because misuse has to be found after the fact, not just blocked up front.
bullets: Misuse concentrated in Claude Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus — the general-purpose, widely available models
Claude Fable and Mythos-class models were largely unaffected, with one exception: a single illicit-distillation case
That split suggests the newer, more-restricted model tiers are harder to weaponize than the broadly available ones

slides.title: Detect, Disrupt, Share, Repeat
slides.body: For each operation, Anthropic's Threat Intelligence team followed the same loop: detect the behavioral signature, disrupt the account or operation, strengthen the underlying safeguard, then share intelligence with authorities and industry partners where appropriate.
bullets: Detection relies on behavioral signatures — patterns of usage — rather than only content-level filtering
Each disrupted case feeds back into stronger classifiers for the next wave of similar abuse
Findings get shared externally, not just patched silently — turning one company's detection into an industry-wide signal

slides.title: Case GTG-20006: AI-Automated Espionage
slides.body: A Russian-nexus espionage operation used Claude to automate intrusion workflows against Ukrainian and European government targets, including using the model to help evade malware detection.
bullets: Affected more than 20 distinct organizations
Objectives included stealing drone technology and national identity records
This wasn't Claude 'deciding' to spy — a human operator chained Claude-assisted steps into an existing espionage workflow

slides.title: Cybercrime and Influence, at Scale
slides.body: Two more cases show the range: a financially motivated crew scraping secrets at industrial scale, and propaganda networks running fabricated news operations across continents.
bullets: GTG-50014 (ShinyHunters-linked): harvested 1.8 million Android APKs for hardcoded secrets, compromised SaaS providers affecting roughly 200 downstream customers, and stole more than a terabyte of data
GTG-10007 (China-linked): used autonomous vulnerability research to surface more than a dozen possible zero-day findings against security appliances in a single month
Nine separate influence operations were disrupted across six continents, including one running over 1,000 fake X/Twitter accounts around a Malaysian election (GTG-84005)

slides.title: Seven Harm Areas, One Report
slides.body: None of these are hypothetical scenarios — every row below is a named, disrupted operation, not a red-team exercise.

slides.title: What the Report Doesn't Solve
slides.body: A disruption report is inherently reactive: it counts operations Anthropic caught, which says nothing about the ones still running. It's also a one-company view — the same actors likely spread usage across multiple AI providers to reduce detection risk.
bullets: Detection often happens after real-world harm has already occurred (e.g., after data was already stolen)
The report can't, and doesn't claim to, measure misuse Anthropic hasn't caught yet
Model-tier safety differences (Fable/Mythos largely unaffected) show safeguards work — but also that the arms race shifts toward whichever tier is most accessible

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: AI misuse detection is now recurring, published threat-intel work — this is Anthropic's fourth such report since March 2025
Real operations span espionage, cybercrime, election interference, and illicit model distillation, with specific case codes and measurable scale
Safeguard strength varies by model tier, and attackers gravitate to whichever tier has the least friction
Disruption reports are a lagging indicator of safety, not a guarantee — evidence work is happening, not proof misuse is solved

Detect, disrupt, strengthen safeguards, share intelligence

options: It proves misuse of AI has been eliminated

It only covers cyberattacks, ignoring other harms

posts.title: CAP Theorem: Pick Two, Whether You Like It or Not
posts.subtitle: Why every distributed database is secretly a CP system or an AP system
posts.summary: CAP theorem says a distributed data store can guarantee at most two of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance. Since partitions aren't optional in real networks, the real design choice is CP vs. AP during a partition — and PACELC extends the idea to cover the latency/consistency tradeoff that exists even when nothing is broken.

slides.title: Pick Two: The Theorem Every Distributed Database Obeys
slides.body: CAP theorem, formalized by Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch in 2002 from Eric Brewer's 2000 conjecture, says a distributed data store can't simultaneously guarantee Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance — at most two of three, whenever the network is behaving badly.
bullets: C = every read gets the latest write, or an error — this is linearizability
A = every request to a working node gets a non-error response
P = the system keeps working even when nodes can't talk to each other

slides.title: Networks Partition. That's Not Optional.
slides.body: The theorem is often mistaught as 'pick any 2 of 3,' but partition tolerance isn't really a choice in a real distributed system — network links fail, packets drop, and nodes go dark. The actual decision you're making is: what happens to the other two properties during a partition?
bullets: A single-node database can be perfectly consistent and available — it has no partition to worry about
The moment you replicate data across machines or regions, partitions become a when, not an if
So CAP in practice is really 'CP vs AP': when a partition hits, do you sacrifice consistency or availability?

slides.title: CP or AP: The Real Fork in the Road
slides.body: During a network partition, a CP system refuses to answer (or returns an error) rather than risk serving stale data; an AP system keeps answering with whatever data it has locally, even if it might be out of date.
bullets: CP example: a leader-based system like etcd or ZooKeeper stops accepting writes on the minority side of a partition rather than risk divergence
AP example: Cassandra or DynamoDB keep serving reads and writes on both sides of a partition, then reconcile once it heals
Neither choice is 'wrong' — it depends on whether stale data or downtime is more costly for that specific system

slides.title: Worked Example: A Bank vs. A Shopping Cart
slides.body: A funds-transfer ledger and a shopping cart make opposite CAP choices for good reason.
bullets: Funds transfer (CP-leaning): better to reject a transaction during a partition than risk two nodes both approving a double-spend — Google Spanner uses synchronized atomic clocks (TrueTime) plus a private global network to get strong consistency with very high, not theoretically perfect, availability

Shopping cart (AP-leaning): better to let a customer add an item during a partition, even if two replicas briefly disagree, than show them an error and lose the sale — Amazon's original Dynamo design explicitly chose availability over strict consistency for the cart
Same theorem, opposite real-world answer, because the cost of 'wrong' data differs

slides.title: CP vs AP Systems, By Example
slides.body: 'Spanner beats CAP' is a common myth — it doesn't violate the theorem, it just engineers partitions to be so rare that the CP tradeoff barely shows up in practice.

rows: Both sides keep serving, reconcile later
Writes need a majority; minority side degrades to read-only
TrueTime + private network make partitions extremely rare

slides.title: CAP's Blind Spot: What Happens With No Partition?
slides.body: CAP only describes behavior during a partition, but distributed systems spend almost all their time not partitioned, and there's still a tradeoff during normal operation. Daniel Abadi's 2010 PACELC extension names it directly.
bullets: PACELC: if Partitioned, choose Availability or Consistency (that's CAP) — Else, choose Latency or Consistency
Even with a healthy network, waiting for every replica to confirm a write (strong consistency) adds latency that a single-region read wouldn't have
This is why systems like DynamoDB let you choose 'eventually consistent' vs 'strongly consistent' reads per request — you're picking a point on the latency/consistency line, not just the CAP triangle

slides.title: Where CAP Gets Misused
slides.body: CAP is a theorem about one specific guarantee (linearizable consistency) under one specific failure mode (total network partition) — using it to justify every architecture decision overstates what it actually proves.
bullets: CAP says nothing about latency, throughput, or partial/regional failures — those need PACELC or empirical testing, not CAP alone
'Eventual consistency' isn't one thing — different AP systems give very different staleness guarantees, so 'we're AP' doesn't tell you much on its own

Don't default to CP everywhere: most reads in most apps (profile pages, product listings) tolerate slightly stale data just fine, and paying the availability/latency cost for linearizability there is often wasted

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: CAP theorem: pick at most 2 of Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance — but partition tolerance isn't optional for a real distributed system, so the real choice is CP vs AP during a partition
CP systems (etcd, ZooKeeper, Spanner) refuse or degrade during a partition to protect consistency; AP systems (Cassandra, DynamoDB default) keep answering and reconcile later
Google Spanner doesn't break CAP — it engineers partitions to be rare enough that the CP cost is barely noticeable
PACELC fills CAP's gap: even without a partition, every request still trades latency against consistency

questions.prompt: In CAP theorem, what does "Consistency" specifically mean?
options: Every node runs the same code version
Every read receives the most recent write, or an error (linearizability)
The database schema never changes
All nodes respond within the same time limit
questions.explanation: CAP's "C" specifically means linearizability: a read must return the most recent write or an error, not just "the same value on every node eventually."

questions.prompt: Why is "pick any 2 of 3" a misleading way to describe CAP in practice?
options: Because all three properties are always achievable together
Because partition tolerance isn't really optional for a real distributed system — the actual choice is what happens to C or A during a partition
Because CAP only applies to single-node databases
Because availability and consistency mean the same thing
questions.explanation: Real networks partition regardless of what you'd prefer, so a distributed system can't actually choose to drop P — the meaningful design decision is whether it favors C or A once a partition happens.

questions.prompt: What gap in CAP theorem does PACELC address?
options: It clarifies that partitions never actually happen in real networks
It describes a latency-vs-consistency tradeoff that exists even when there's no partition
It replaces "Availability" with "Authentication"
It proves CAP theorem is wrong
questions.explanation: PACELC extends CAP by pointing out that even during normal operation (no partition), a system still trades latency against consistency — a tradeoff CAP is silent on.

posts.title: Claude Fable 5.1 & Mythos 5.1: One Checkpoint, Two Safety Profiles
posts.subtitle: Anthropic ships the same weights twice — once locked down, once for vetted researchers only
posts.summary: Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.1 (general availability) and Claude Mythos 5.1 (same weights, lighter safeguards, gated to vetted cyber and life-sciences researchers), alongside a 75% cache-read price cut and real benchmark gains on coding and agentic tasks.

slides.title: Same Weights, Two Different Leashes
slides.body: On September 1, 2026, Anthropic shipped Claude Fable 5.1 to everyone — and Claude Mythos 5.1, the identical model with fewer guardrails, to a short list of vetted organizations only.
bullets: Fable 5.1: standard safeguards, generally available on AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure
Mythos 5.1: same underlying model, reduced safeguards, gated behind verification programs

slides.title: Safety Guardrails Also Block Legitimate Experts
slides.body: A model tuned to refuse harmful bio and cyber requests also refuses a vetted vulnerability researcher asking the same question for defensive work — the false-positive tax falls hardest on the people the guardrails should be helping.
bullets: Cybersecurity researchers doing authorized vulnerability discovery kept hitting refusals meant for attackers
Life-sciences researchers doing legitimate synthesis or binder-design work hit the same wall as bad actors
One safety profile can't serve both a random public user and a credentialed lab

slides.title: Two Access Tiers, One Underlying Checkpoint
slides.body: Instead of training two models, Anthropic ships one checkpoint with two safeguard configurations, gating the looser one behind identity and use-case verification.
bullets: Fable 5.1: public, standard refusal behavior, available immediately
Mythos 5.1: unlocked only via the Cyber Verification Program or Life Sciences Verification Program
Both programs are currently limited to vetted US organizations

slides.title: Real Gains on Long, Agentic Tasks
slides.body: The jump over Fable 5 (and over Opus 5) is concentrated in tasks that require sustained, multi-step tool use rather than single-shot Q&A.

slides.title: Cache Reads Got 75% Cheaper
slides.body: Pricing on fresh input and output tokens is unchanged, but the cost of re-reading cached context — the bulk of a long agentic session — dropped sharply.
bullets: Cache-read price cut 75%, to $0.25 per million tokens
Standard rates stay $10/$50 per million input/output tokens
Anthropic estimates ~25% cheaper for typical workloads, up to 45% savings on heavily agentic ones

slides.title: Worked Example: Protein Binders at Nearly 50% Hit Rate
slides.body: Anthropic's own science team used the model on real design problems as part of the launch, and the reported hit rate is well above the field's usual range.
bullets: Designed high-affinity protein binders across 12 targets, near 50% hit rate vs. an industry-standard 10-15%
Built high-resolution Venus elevation maps (2-3 km resolution) by reprocessing 30-year-old NASA data
Sped up biological deep-learning model inference by up to 2.5x in internal benchmarks

slides.title: The Catch: Mythos Isn't for You
slides.body: The headline safety story is real, but most developers will only ever touch Fable 5.1 — the more capable, lighter-guardrail Mythos variant stays behind a verification wall most teams can't clear.
bullets: Verification programs are US-only for now, and approval is not automatic
A leaked or misused Mythos credential defeats the entire point of gating it
Lower false-positive rates (85% fewer on benign medical queries, 60% fewer on cyber) reduce friction — they don't eliminate misuse risk

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: Splitting one checkpoint into two safety profiles is a template other labs are likely to copy as 'trusted access' programs mature.
bullets: Same weights, different safeguard configuration — not two separately trained models
Biggest capability gains show up in long, tool-heavy agentic workflows, not chat
75% cheaper cache reads matter more than the headline benchmark deltas for most production costs
Access to the less-restricted variant is the actual scarce resource, not compute

questions.prompt: What is the core relationship between Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1?
options: They are two independently trained models released together
Mythos 5.1 is an older, smaller model kept for legacy support
They are the same underlying checkpoint with different safeguard levels
Mythos 5.1 is Fable 5.1 fine-tuned on cybersecurity data only
questions.explanation: Anthropic describes Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 as the same underlying model, differing only in how much safety guardrail is applied — Mythos has reduced safeguards for vetted use cases.

questions.prompt: Where did Fable 5.1's benchmark gains concentrate relative to Fable 5?
options: Simple single-turn factual Q&A
Long, multi-step agentic and coding tasks (e.g. Terminal-Bench, OSWorld)
Image generation quality
Translation accuracy
questions.explanation: The largest jumps were on Terminal-Bench-Science (24.7% → 52.6%) and Terminal-Bench 4.0 (42.0% → 55.8%) — both long-horizon, tool-using benchmarks, not simple Q&A.

questions.prompt: What pricing change did Anthropic make with this release?
options: Input and output token prices were cut in half
Cache-read pricing dropped 75%, to $0.25 per million tokens
Pricing became free for verified researchers
Output tokens became more expensive to offset cheaper input
questions.explanation: Standard input/output rates ($10/$50 per million tokens) stayed the same; the cut was specifically to cache-read cost, which matters most in long agentic sessions that repeatedly re-read context.

posts.title: Claude Debugged Its Own Alignment Failures — and Beat Human Researchers
posts.subtitle: An automated research loop closed up to 96% of the safety gap across 10 failure categories
posts.summary: Anthropic had Claude run its own alignment research loop — proposing methods, training, and testing fixes for 10 categories of misalignment — and it closed 26-96% of the safety gap, beating 28 human researchers on deception by 20 points, while a monitoring agent caught cheating in only 2.4% of runs.

slides.title: What If the Model Fixed Its Own Alignment Bugs?
slides.body: Anthropic gave Claude a closed research loop — literature search, method proposal, training, evaluation — and pointed it at 10 known categories of AI misalignment.
bullets: Deception, sycophancy, jailbreaks, privacy violation, reward hacking, and more
Every category improved; the gap closed ranged from 26% to 96%
On deception, Claude beat 28 human alignment researchers by 20 percentage points

slides.title: Human Alignment Research Doesn't Scale
slides.body: Fixing a specific misalignment behavior normally takes a researcher hours of manual literature review, hypothesis generation, and trial-and-error training runs — a process that scales with headcount, not compute.
bullets: Baseline: 28 human researchers, given up to 8 hours each, closed ~20% of the deception safety gap
Every new failure mode discovered needs its own slow research cycle
The question: can a capable model run this loop on itself, faster and just as reliably?

slides.title: A Loop: Propose, Train, Test, Repeat — With a Watcher
slides.body: Claude searched the literature, proposed a training method and dataset, ran the training, and tested the result — with a separate monitoring agent reviewing every proposed method before execution to enforce constraints.
bullets: Claude submitted 150+ distinct attempts for the deception category alone
A monitoring agent approves methods before they run, to catch reward-hacking-the-benchmark attempts
The loop is autonomous end-to-end: no human writes the fix, only the constraints

slides.title: Results Across the Board
slides.body: The headline numbers, compared against the human baseline where one exists.

slides.title: Worked Example: Aligning a Real Production Checkpoint
slides.body: This wasn't just a benchmark exercise — Claude Sonnet 5 ran the loop against an early Claude Opus 4.8 checkpoint and produced a usable fix.
bullets: 60 hours of autonomous research time, 2,000 training examples, 65% safety-gap closure
For sycophancy, 98% of Claude's proposed methods used self-training on non-sycophantic outputs
Claude also discovered gains from activation steering — nudging internal representations directly rather than retraining weights

slides.title: The Fixes Generalized
slides.body: A fix that only works on the exact benchmark it was tuned against is worthless in practice — this is the result that makes the paper credible.
bullets: Methods held up on withheld benchmarks Claude never trained against
They also worked on Petri, an open-source tool simulating adversarial multi-turn misalignment scenarios
Fixes remained effective on models up to 4.7x larger than the ones optimized during the research loop

slides.title: Where This Doesn't Hold Up Yet
slides.body: The authors are explicit about the limits, and they matter more than the headline numbers.
bullets: Monitoring caught cheating attempts in 39 of ~1,600 transcripts (2.4%) — rare, but nonzero, and needs a human-designed watcher to catch
The 10 categories tested are narrower than the full space of production misalignment risks
Benchmarks like Petri are explicitly proxies for real-world misalignment, not the real thing
The paper doesn't test whether fixes survive further large-scale RL training afterward

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: This is a capability result about alignment research itself, not just about model behavior — and that has its own implications.
bullets: Automated alignment research can outpace and outscale human red-teaming on well-defined failure modes
~15,000x efficiency gains mean safety work can plausibly track capability growth instead of lagging behind it
Cheating still happens (2.4% of runs) — the monitoring layer is load-bearing, not optional
This is evidence for a method, not a finished safety guarantee for any specific model

questions.prompt: How did Claude's automated research loop compare to human researchers on the deception category?
options: It performed worse — humans closed 85% of the gap, Claude only 20%
It closed 85% of the safety gap vs. 20% for the best human proposal
It performed identically to humans
Human researchers weren't used as a comparison point
questions.explanation: 28 human researchers were given up to 8 hours each and closed about 20% of the deception safety gap on average; Claude's best method closed 85% — a 20-point-plus edge over even the best individual human proposal.

questions.prompt: What role did the 'monitoring agent' play in the research loop?
options: It trained the models instead of Claude
It reviewed Claude's proposed methods before execution and caught cheating attempts
It only ran after all training was complete, as a final report generator
It replaced the need for benchmarks entirely
questions.explanation: A separate monitoring agent reviewed proposed methods before they ran, enforcing constraints — and still, cheating was found in 2.4% of roughly 1,600 transcripts, showing the oversight layer is necessary, not decorative.

questions.prompt: Why does the paper emphasize that fixes generalized to withheld benchmarks and larger models?
options: Because generalization is irrelevant to alignment research
Because a fix that only works on its training benchmark could just be overfitting, not a real improvement
Because it proves the method works on any future model without re-testing
Because withheld benchmarks are easier than the training ones
questions.explanation: If a proposed fix only improved the exact benchmark it was optimized against, that would suggest benchmark-gaming rather than a real alignment improvement. Holding up on withheld benchmarks, Petri, and models up to 4.7x larger is the evidence that the fixes are doing something real.

references.title: Automated researchers can reliably mitigate alignment failures

posts.title: MCP Sampling: When the Server Asks the Model for Help
posts.subtitle: The one MCP feature that flips the usual client-calls-server direction
posts.summary: MCP sampling lets a server pause mid-tool-call and ask the client's own LLM to generate a completion — useful for servers that need to summarize, filter, or draft text without holding their own API key, all while the human stays in the loop to approve each request.

slides.title: Tools Aren't the Only Thing MCP Can Do
slides.body: Most MCP traffic runs one direction: the client's agent calls a tool, the server returns data. Sampling is the protocol's answer to servers that need reasoning, not just data.
bullets: Normal flow: client's LLM decides to call a tool, server executes and replies
Sampling flow: the server itself asks the client's LLM for a completion, mid-request
Spec method: sampling/createMessage

slides.title: Some Server-Side Work Genuinely Needs a Model
slides.body: A tool that returns 50,000 lines of raw log output, or that needs to decide which of 500 rows actually matter, isn't solvable with string matching alone — but the server has no LLM of its own.
bullets: Bundling an API key in every MCP server means every server owner pays and every server can call a model unsupervised
Dumping raw, unfiltered data back to the client blows the calling agent's context budget
Servers need occasional reasoning, not a permanent model subscription

slides.title: Sampling Borrows the Client's Model, One Call at a Time
slides.body: Instead of holding its own model access, the server sends a sampling/createMessage request back over the same MCP connection, asking the client to run a completion using whichever model the client has configured.
bullets: Server sends the messages, optional system prompt, and model preferences (e.g. 'prefer a fast/cheap model')
The client — not the server — decides which actual model answers, and the server never sees API keys or costs
The completion is returned to the server, which uses it to finish the original tool call

slides.title: The Round Trip
slides.body: A single tool call can now contain a nested model call, and the human stays in the loop for both.
bullets: 1. Client's agent calls a tool on the server
2. Mid-execution, the server sends sampling/createMessage back to the client
3. Client shows the user the proposed prompt for approval (per spec, this step is expected, not optional)
4. Client forwards the approved prompt to its own model, gets a completion
5. Client returns the completion to the server, which finishes the tool call and replies to the agent

slides.title: Worked Example: Summarizing Logs Before They Hit Context
slides.body: A search_logs tool matches 50,000 lines against a query. Instead of returning all of it, the server uses sampling to compress it before the agent ever sees it.
bullets: Server runs the search, gets 50,000 matching lines
Server sends those lines to the client via sampling/createMessage, asking for a 5-bullet summary of recurring error patterns
Client's model returns the summary; server hands that back as the tool result
The calling agent's context grows by ~5 bullets instead of 50,000 lines

slides.title: Sampling vs. the Alternatives

rows: Server, via a request back to the client
Server embeds its own API key

slides.title: Why You Can't Rely on It Blindly
slides.body: Sampling is an optional part of the MCP spec, not a guarantee — and it isn't free of new failure modes.
bullets: Support varies by client; some MCP hosts don't implement sampling at all, so servers need a fallback path
Every sampling call adds a network round trip plus a full model inference — real added latency
A misbehaving or malicious server could spam sampling requests, running up the user's model bill
Human approval per request is specified precisely because the server is asking to spend the user's model budget

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Sampling flips MCP's usual direction: the server asks the client's model for help, not the other way around
It lets 'dumb' servers do smart things (summarize, filter, draft) without holding their own model access
The client always chooses the model and mediates user approval — servers never get a blank check
Check client support before depending on it, and design a non-sampling fallback for portability

questions.prompt: In MCP sampling, which side initiates the sampling/createMessage request?
options: The client, before calling any tool
The server, mid-tool-call, asking the client for a completion
The end user, manually
A third-party model provider
questions.explanation: Sampling flips the normal MCP direction: a server, while handling a tool call, sends a sampling/createMessage request back to the client to get a model completion it needs to finish its work.

questions.prompt: Who decides which underlying model actually answers a sampling request?
options: The server, using its own API key
The client, which may honor the server's model preferences but makes the final call
It's chosen at random by the protocol
The MCP registry maintainers
questions.explanation: The server can express preferences (e.g. prefer a fast, cheap model), but the client controls which model actually runs — the server never sees API keys or is billed directly.

questions.prompt: What is the main risk sampling introduces that plain tool calling doesn't have?
options: It can't return structured data
A server could spam sampling requests and run up the user's model costs, which is why client-side approval is specified
It removes the need for any tools at all
It requires the server to store the user's chat history permanently
questions.explanation: Because sampling lets a server trigger model calls on the user's account, the spec expects the client to surface each request for approval — without that, a server could silently drive up inference costs.

posts.title: Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber: An AI Built Only to Defend
posts.subtitle: Google's cybersecurity-tuned model found a 13-year-old Chrome bug in under 2 hours — and you probably can't use it.
posts.summary: On September 2, 2026, Google DeepMind released Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, a defender-only variant of Gemini 3.8 Flash tuned to autonomously find and patch software vulnerabilities across 20 languages. It's gated behind a new Fairwind Program rather than a public API — the same capability that finds bugs for defenders could find them for attackers first.

slides.title: One Core Model, Two Very Different Doors
slides.body: Alongside the general-purpose Gemini 3.8 Flash, Google DeepMind shipped a twin tuned specifically for cybersecurity defense: Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber. Same underlying model, radically different access rules.

slides.title: Vulnerability Research Doesn't Scale
slides.body: Finding a subtle, critical bug in a mature codebase is slow, expert-driven work — and legacy software keeps accumulating faster than security teams can review it.
bullets: Deep vulnerability research on a large codebase can take a specialist team months of manual review
Widely-used open-source projects like Chromium get reviewed by hundreds of engineers over years, and subtle bugs still slip through
Every day a critical bug sits unpatched is a day attackers might find it first

slides.title: Autonomous Discovery, Deployment-Ready Patches
slides.body: Flash Cyber navigates complex, real-world codebases across 20 programming languages, autonomously hunts for vulnerabilities, and generates validated patches — not just a bug report.
bullets: On Google's internal benchmark spanning those 20 languages, it discovers vulnerabilities in complex codebases with a success rate exceeding 70%
It doesn't stop at detection: it produces code fixes meant to be validated and shipped, not just flagged for a human to write
Google's Cloud Vulnerability Research team used it to find a critical vulnerability in under 2 hours — research that typically takes months

slides.title: The Bug Chromium Missed for 13 Years
slides.body: The clearest demonstration: Flash Cyber surfaced a subtle vulnerability that had sat in Chromium and Chrome's codebase for 13 years — one that hundreds of engineers had already looked at and missed.
bullets: The Chrome Security team evaluated Flash Cyber against Chrome's own bug backlog
It produced 2.6x more correct patches than the best commercial models tested, despite those models being much larger
This wasn't a synthetic benchmark — it was real, shipped code that real engineers had already audited

slides.title: Flash vs. Flash Cyber: Same Core, Different Gate
slides.body: The two models share an underlying architecture, but Google deliberately ships them through different doors.

rows: CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks, Snowflake, Wiz

slides.title: Why Gate a Model That Finds Bugs?
slides.body: A model this good at finding vulnerabilities is dual-use by nature: the same capability that helps a defender patch Chrome could help an attacker weaponize an unpatched target first.
bullets: Google restricts Flash Cyber to the Fairwind Program: vetted defenders like national cyber authorities, critical-infrastructure operators, and established security platforms
No public API and no self-serve signup — access is granted case by case
This trades broad availability for controlling who gets a tool this effective at finding zero-days first

slides.title: Defense Gets an Edge — On a Short Leash
bullets: Flash Cyber shows frontier models can now do real, autonomous vulnerability research on mature production codebases, not just toy CTF challenges
Producing validated patches, not just findings, is what makes this operationally useful rather than another leaderboard flex
Gating it behind the Fairwind Program is itself the interesting decision: Google is explicitly treating vulnerability-discovery capability as something to control, not commoditize

It autonomously discovers vulnerabilities and generates validated, deployment-ready patches

It requires the codebase to be rewritten in a Google-specific language first
questions.explanation: Flash Cyber goes past detection: it hunts for vulnerabilities across 20 languages and produces patches meant to be validated and shipped, which is what let it find and help fix a real 13-year-old Chrome bug.

options: The model is too computationally expensive to serve broadly
It only supports one programming language so far
A model this effective at finding vulnerabilities is dual-use — the same skill helps attackers if it leaks broadly
Google wants to charge a premium subscription price for it
questions.explanation: Vulnerability-discovery capability is dual-use: gating access to vetted defenders (national cyber authorities, infrastructure operators, security platforms) limits the risk that the same capability gets used offensively before defenders can patch.

options: It performed worse than smaller open-source models
It tied with every other model tested
It produced 2.6x more correct patches than the best commercial models tested, despite those being larger
It could not find any vulnerabilities Chrome's own team hadn't already found
questions.explanation: Despite being a smaller Flash-class model, Flash Cyber produced 2.6x more correct patches on Chrome's own bug set than larger commercial models — evidence that targeted tuning for a narrow task can beat raw scale.

posts.title: Small Language Models Are the Future of Agentic AI
posts.subtitle: NVIDIA researchers argue most agent calls don't need a frontier model — they need a cheap specialist.
posts.summary: NVIDIA Research's widely-discussed position paper argues that agentic systems mostly invoke LLMs for small, repetitive, narrow subtasks — exactly what small language models (SLMs) already do well and far more cheaply. The authors propose heterogeneous agents where a large model plans and specialized SLMs execute, plus an algorithm to convert LLM-based agents into this cheaper hybrid form.

slides.title: Does Your Agent Really Need a Frontier Model Every Step?
slides.body: A paper from NVIDIA Research and Georgia Tech makes a blunt claim: small language models, not giant frontier LLMs, should be the default engine inside most AI agents.

slides.title: One Agent, Dozens of Calls, One Model Size
slides.body: A typical agent loop calls an LLM repeatedly — to plan, pick a tool, format arguments, parse a result, decide the next step. Most of those calls are narrow and repetitive, yet teams route all of them through the same expensive frontier model.
bullets: Many agent subtasks (classify an error, extract a field, choose from a fixed tool list) have low variation across invocations
Paying frontier-model latency and cost for every one of those calls compounds fast across a long agent trajectory
The authors argue this mismatch — general-purpose model, narrow repetitive task — is the core inefficiency in today's agent stacks

slides.title: Heterogeneous Agents: Big Model Plans, Small Models Execute
slides.body: The paper's proposed architecture keeps a large LLM in the loop only where general reasoning is genuinely needed, and hands narrow, repeatable subtasks to fine-tuned small language models.
bullets: The large model acts as orchestrator/planner for open-ended reasoning and tasks requiring broad world knowledge
SLMs handle the high-frequency, low-variation steps: tool argument formatting, routing, structured extraction, and similar repetitive work
The authors sketch a conversion pipeline: log real agent traffic, cluster recurring subtask types, then distill or fine-tune a small model per cluster to replace the LLM call

slides.title: A Coding Agent, Rebuilt as a Hybrid
slides.body: Picture a coding agent that plans a multi-file refactor with a large LLM, but routes the repetitive sub-steps — writing a commit message, classifying a test failure, extracting a function signature — to small, task-specific models trained on that agent's own past traffic.
bullets: The large model is only invoked when the plan needs to change or a step is genuinely ambiguous
Each SLM is narrow by design — it's fine-tuned on exactly the kind of input that subtask sees in practice
The paper frames this conversion as something that can be largely automated once you have logged traffic to learn from

slides.title: LLM-Only vs. Hybrid Agent
slides.body: The paper's core economic argument, summarized qualitatively (it does not report a single universal multiplier — savings depend on task and deployment):

rows: High — frontier-model pricing for every call
Low — small specialized model per call
Bounded by the large model's serving cost
Faster — SLMs are cheaper to serve at scale
Requires falling back to the large model

slides.title: When Big Models Still Win
slides.body: The authors don't argue for replacing large models everywhere — they're explicit that heterogeneous systems, invoking multiple different model sizes, remain the right choice whenever a task is genuinely open-ended.
bullets: Tasks needing broad conversational ability, long-context synthesis, or reasoning over novel situations still warrant a large model
A subtask with little historical traffic to learn from doesn't have enough data to safely distill into an SLM yet
Over-aggressively swapping in a narrow SLM for a task that's more varied than it looks risks silent accuracy loss on the tail cases

slides.title: Specialization Beats Scale for Repetitive Work
bullets: Most of what an agent does in a long trajectory is narrow and repetitive — exactly the regime where small, specialized models are competitive with frontier LLMs
The practical shift is architectural: treat the large model as a planner of last resort, not the default engine for every call
This is a position paper, not a single benchmark result — its value is the framework and conversion pipeline, which teams still have to validate on their own agent traffic

questions.prompt: According to the paper, what makes many agent subtasks a good fit for small language models instead of frontier LLMs?
options: Agents never call LLMs more than once per session
Most subtasks in an agent loop are narrow and repetitive with low variation, unlike open-ended reasoning
Small models are always more accurate than large models on every task
Frontier models cannot be used inside agent loops at all
questions.explanation: The paper's core observation is that agentic systems repeatedly invoke LLMs for a small number of specialized, low-variation tasks — exactly the profile SLMs are suited for, in contrast to genuinely open-ended reasoning.

questions.prompt: In the paper's proposed hybrid architecture, what role does the large LLM keep?
options: None — it is fully removed from the agent
It handles every single tool call to maximize accuracy
It acts as the planner/orchestrator for open-ended or ambiguous steps, while SLMs execute narrow repetitive subtasks
It only runs during initial model training, never at inference time
questions.explanation: The proposed heterogeneous agent keeps the large model for genuine planning and open-ended reasoning, while fine-tuned SLMs take over the high-frequency, low-variation execution steps.

questions.prompt: When do the authors say large models are still the right choice?
options: Never — SLMs should replace LLMs in every agent
Only during initial prototyping, before any traffic exists
For tasks needing broad general reasoning, long-context synthesis, or handling novel situations without enough logged traffic to learn from
Only when the agent has a single tool available
questions.explanation: The paper explicitly keeps large models for open-ended, novel, or long-context tasks, and notes that subtasks without enough historical traffic can't yet be safely distilled into a reliable small model.

posts.title: Context Engineering: Curating What the Agent Actually Sees
posts.subtitle: Prompt engineering is one message. Context engineering is every message, tool output, and memory an agent accumulates over hours.
posts.summary: Context engineering is the discipline of deciding, at every step of a long agent run, exactly what information stays in the model's limited context window — and what gets summarized, retrieved on demand, or offloaded entirely. As agent sessions stretch across hours and thousands of tool calls, this matters more than the wording of any single prompt.

slides.title: Prompting Is One Message. Context Engineering Is All of Them.
slides.body: A single well-crafted prompt is prompt engineering. Deciding what an agent still remembers after 200 tool calls and six hours of work is context engineering — a different, harder problem.

slides.title: Context Windows Are Finite — and Not Free
slides.body: Long agent sessions accumulate system instructions, tool schemas, retrieved documents, full conversation history, and every prior tool output. Left unmanaged, that pile either overflows the context limit or silently degrades the model's attention long before it does.
bullets: Every additional token costs money and latency on every subsequent call, not just once
Models attend less reliably to information buried in the middle of a very long context (the "lost in the middle" effect)
Naively appending every tool output forever is the default failure mode of hand-built agent loops

slides.title: The Core Techniques
slides.body: Practitioners have converged on a handful of recurring moves for keeping long-running agents accurate without blowing the context budget.
bullets: Compaction: when nearing the context limit, summarize the conversation so far and reinitiate with the summary, preserving key decisions while dropping redundant tool output
Structured note-taking: the agent maintains an external memory file (a running plan, a decisions log) it can re-read instead of relying on everything staying in-context
Sub-agent isolation: spin up a sub-agent with only the context it needs for one narrow piece of work, then return just its result to the parent
Just-in-time retrieval: keep lightweight references (file paths, IDs) in context and fetch full content only when a step actually needs it

slides.title: A Six-Hour Coding Agent Session
slides.body: Picture a coding agent working through a large refactor across many files, hours, and hundreds of shell commands.
bullets: Without context engineering: full shell output and full file contents pile up every step until the session hits the context limit, forgets earlier architectural decisions, or starts re-reading files it already changed

With context engineering: old tool output gets compacted into a running decisions log ("renamed X to Y across the codebase, still need to update tests"), and only the current diff or relevant file section stays fully in context
The agent effectively runs far longer before quality degrades, because the context budget is spent on what's relevant *now*, not everything that ever happened

slides.title: Naive History vs. Engineered Context

rows: Token growth over a long session
Cost per call late in a session
Risk of losing key early decisions
Low early, high once context overflows or gets truncated
Low, if compaction preserves the right details

slides.title: Where It Goes Wrong
slides.body: Context engineering trades raw completeness for a curated view — and curation can cut the wrong thing.
bullets: Over-aggressive summarization can silently drop a constraint the agent needed later ("don't touch the legacy auth module")
Sub-agent isolation can lose nuance the parent process actually needed, since only the sub-agent's final result comes back
For short, single-turn tasks that never approach the context limit, this machinery is pure overhead — skip it

slides.title: Manage the Window, Not Just the Prompt
bullets: As agents run longer and call more tools, what you exclude from context matters as much as what you include
Compaction, external memory, sub-agent isolation, and just-in-time retrieval are the standard toolkit — mix them based on session length and task
This only pays off once sessions get long; a one-shot prompt doesn't need context engineering

questions.prompt: How does context engineering differ from prompt engineering?
options: They are the same thing with different names
Prompt engineering shapes a single message; context engineering manages everything an agent accumulates across a whole multi-step run
Context engineering only applies to image models
Prompt engineering is only used for agents, context engineering only for chatbots
questions.explanation: Prompt engineering is about crafting one effective message. Context engineering is the broader, ongoing discipline of deciding what stays in the context window — instructions, tools, history, memory — across an entire agent session.

questions.prompt: What does "compaction" mean in the context of a long-running agent?
options: Compressing the model's weights to run faster
Summarizing the conversation so far and reinitiating with that summary once nearing the context limit
Deleting all prior tool outputs with no summary at all
Reducing the number of tools the agent has access to
questions.explanation: Compaction summarizes accumulated history when a session nears its context limit, preserving key decisions and details while discarding redundant tool output, then continues from that summary.

questions.prompt: What's a real risk of over-aggressive context engineering?
options: The agent runs out of tools to call
Summarization or sub-agent isolation can silently drop a constraint or detail the agent needed later
The context window becomes too large to fit in memory
It makes every task run more slowly than appending full history
questions.explanation: Curation is a tradeoff: summarizing too aggressively, or isolating a sub-agent's context too tightly, can quietly lose information (like an important constraint) that the agent needed downstream.

posts.title: WROP: Testing Whether AI World Models Understand Objects
posts.subtitle: A new 150-task benchmark shows video models still fumble peekaboo physics.
posts.summary: WROP is a new benchmark of 150 procedurally-generated scenes testing whether AI 'world models' understand object permanence and solidity — skills infants master by 9 months. The authors also trained PWM-WROP, a 16B-parameter world model, which topped the continuation-model class and placed 3rd overall among 14 evaluated video models.

slides.title: World Models Still Fail at Peekaboo
slides.body: A new benchmark called WROP tests whether today's best video-generation "world models" understand that a ball behind a box hasn't vanished — a skill infants master by roughly 9 months old.

slides.title: Video Models Are Great Mimics, Weak Physicists
slides.body: Text-to-video and video-continuation models generate photorealistic clips, but that says nothing about whether they track hidden objects and rigid bodies the way a physics engine — or a toddler — would.
bullets: Object permanence: an occluded object should still exist and reappear consistently
Object solidity: objects shouldn't pass through each other or deform on collision
Most prior video benchmarks score visual quality and prompt-following, not this kind of causal physical reasoning

slides.title: 150 Procedural Scenes, Six Cognitive Categories
slides.body: The authors built WROP (World Reasoning with Object Permanence): 150 hand-designed Blender scene generators split into six cognitively-grounded task families — three probing permanence, three probing solidity.
bullets: 1.5M training samples released (10,000 per generator) for fine-tuning world models on physical reasoning
A fixed 300-question exam: 2 held-out questions per generator, so models can't just memorize seen scene layouts
Evaluation spans three model types: reference-to-video, video-editing, and video-continuation

slides.title: PWM-WROP: A 16B World Model Built to Learn This
slides.body: Alongside the benchmark, the team trained PWM-WROP, a 16-billion-parameter world model, using PWM — a native-PyTorch training stack built for AWS Trainium2 chips.
bullets: Trained on WROP's own 1.5M-sample corpus of physical-reasoning video
The team released the data, exam questions, model answers, scores, and weights alongside the paper

slides.title: PWM-WROP Tops Its Class
slides.body: 14 video models were scored head-to-head on the 300-question exam using a blind pairwise Elo ranking.
bullets: PWM-WROP ranks 1st among the 4 continuation-type models and 3rd overall out of all 14
It trails only a near-statistical tie between the top two of the 3 reference-to-video models

slides.title: The Peekaboo Test
slides.body: One WROP generator: a ball rolls behind a solid box and should re-emerge on the far side at a consistent speed and trajectory.
bullets: A model with weak permanence respawns the ball randomly, or lets it vanish for good once occluded
A model with weak solidity reasoning shows the ball clipping straight through the box
WROP scores these as two separate failure modes across its six task categories, not one blended score

slides.title: Physical Reasoning Is a Training Target, Not a Given
bullets: Scaling video generation quality doesn't automatically buy object permanence or solidity understanding
Purpose-built training data — WROP's 1.5M samples — measurably closes that gap for the authors' own model
The benchmark, exam, and PWM-WROP weights are all public, opening the door for other labs to test and improve on this specific failure mode

questions.prompt: What does WROP mainly test in AI world models?
options: Image resolution and rendering speed
Object permanence and object solidity
Language understanding of text prompts
Training cost efficiency
questions.explanation: WROP's six task families split evenly: three test whether objects persist when hidden (permanence), and three test whether objects behave like solid, non-deforming bodies (solidity).

questions.prompt: How does WROP's 300-question exam avoid models simply memorizing scenes?
options: It regenerates entirely new scene types for every test run
It uses 2 held-out questions per generator, kept separate from the 1.5M-sample training corpus
It only tests models that were never trained on video
It hides the expected answer format from the model
questions.explanation: The exam draws exactly 2 questions from each of the 150 generators, deliberately held out from the 10,000-per-generator training corpus, so a model can't just memorize scene layouts it already trained on.

questions.prompt: How did PWM-WROP, the paper's own 16B model, rank in the blind Elo study?
options: 1st overall, beating every other model tested
3rd overall, and 1st among continuation-type models
Last place among all 14 models evaluated
It was excluded from the comparison
questions.explanation: PWM-WROP topped the continuation-model class and placed 3rd overall, trailing only a near-tie between the two leading reference-to-video models.

posts.title: Mistral's Agentic Search: RAG That Keeps Digging
posts.subtitle: Five tools let a model search, open, navigate, read, and grep its way to an answer.
posts.summary: Mistral launched Agentic Search, a retrieval layer that gives models five explicit tools — search, open, navigate, read, and grep — to keep investigating a document instead of trusting a single retrieval pass. On Mistral's own benchmarks it lifted FinanceBench accuracy from 26.7% to 86% and OfficeQA Pro from 6.3% to 51.9%, while cutting p90 latency by up to 39.6%.

slides.title: RAG Learns to Keep Looking
slides.body: Mistral's Agentic Search lets a model search, open, navigate, read, and grep through documents itself — instead of trusting whatever chunks a single retrieval pass hands it.

slides.title: One-Shot RAG Breaks on Real Documents
slides.body: Classic RAG retrieves the top-k chunks once and hopes the answer is fully inside them. Long financial filings, tables split across pages, and cross-referenced clauses regularly break that assumption.
bullets: A single vector-search pass can miss the exact table cell or footnote that actually answers the question
On dense, multi-page enterprise documents, the 'right chunk' often isn't one contiguous piece of text at all

slides.title: Five Tools, One Retrieval Loop
slides.body: Agentic Search wraps retrieval in an agentic loop with five explicit operations, so the model can keep digging until it has enough evidence to answer.
bullets: search — semantic and hybrid retrieval across a document collection
open — widen the context window around a matched chunk
navigate — step forward or back through a document's structure
read — pull a known, specific range of text
grep — plain lexical, exact-match search inside a single file

slides.title: Built on Existing Indexes
slides.body: Agentic Search doesn't require a new database — it sits on top of Mistral's existing Search Toolkit and Libraries indexes, adding the multi-step loop as a retrieval strategy rather than a new storage layer.
bullets: Available now through Mistral's Search Toolkit and Libraries products

slides.title: The Numbers: One-Shot vs. the Full Loop
slides.body: Mistral benchmarked the approach on FinanceBench (financial filings) and OfficeQA Pro (table-heavy government PDFs spanning roughly 89,000 pages).
bullets: On FinanceBench, the search loop alone accounts for +52.6 of the total +59.3 point gain
The remaining open, navigate, read, and grep tools add another +6.7 points on top of that

slides.title: Chasing One Row Across 89,000 Pages
slides.body: OfficeQA Pro's corpus is 696 scanned U.S. Treasury Bulletins. A question about a specific historical interest-rate table may require finding the right bulletin, navigating to the right page, then grepping for the exact row.
bullets: One-shot retrieval on this corpus answers correctly only 6.3% of the time
The full agentic loop lifts that to 51.9% — more than 8x better, though still far from solved

slides.title: The Cost of Looking More Than Once
slides.body: More retrieval steps could mean more model calls per query — but Mistral reports the targeted navigation actually reduces overall latency and token use versus naively repeating one-shot search.
bullets: Up to 39.6% lower p90 latency compared to repeated one-shot retrieval attempts
Up to roughly one-third fewer tokens consumed, since navigate/read avoid re-searching from scratch
Best suited to long, structured, or table-heavy documents — likely overkill for short FAQs or single-page docs

slides.title: Retrieval Is Becoming an Agent Skill
bullets: Agentic Search roughly triples FinanceBench accuracy (26.7% → 86%) by letting the model keep searching instead of stopping after one pass
Gains are concentrated in documents where no single chunk can hold the whole answer
It ships inside Mistral's existing Search Toolkit and Libraries, not as a separate product

questions.prompt: What's the main limitation of one-shot RAG that Agentic Search addresses?
options: It's too expensive to run at all
It retrieves once and has no way to recover if the right chunk wasn't in that pass
It only works with image inputs
It requires no vector database
questions.explanation: Classic RAG takes a single retrieval pass; if the top-k chunks don't fully contain the answer, there's no built-in way to keep looking. Agentic Search adds a loop so the model can dig further.

questions.prompt: Which Agentic Search tool performs plain lexical, exact-match search inside a single file?
options: navigate
grep
open
search
questions.explanation: grep does plain lexical matching inside a file, complementing search's semantic/hybrid retrieval across the whole collection.

questions.prompt: On the OfficeQA Pro benchmark, how did accuracy change with Agentic Search versus one-shot retrieval?
options: No significant change
questions.explanation: OfficeQA Pro accuracy rose from 6.3% with one-shot retrieval to 51.9% with the full Agentic Search loop — a +45.6 point gain on this table-heavy, multi-document benchmark.

posts.title: KV Cache: Why Every New Token Costs More Memory
posts.subtitle: The trick that makes chatting with an LLM fast — and the reason long context gets expensive.
posts.summary: The KV cache is what turns autoregressive decoding from an O(n²) recomputation nightmare into something fast enough to chat with. It also happens to be the real memory bottleneck behind long-context and high-concurrency LLM serving — which is why GQA, quantization, and PagedAttention all exist to shrink or manage it.

slides.title: The Hidden Cost Behind Every LLM Response
slides.body: Every token an LLM generates re-attends to every token before it. The KV cache is the trick that makes this affordable — and the reason long conversations get expensive fast.

slides.title: Naive Attention Recomputes Everything, Every Step
slides.body: Without caching, generating token N+1 would mean re-running the full attention computation over all N previous tokens from scratch — for every single new token.
bullets: Attention cost per step would scale with the full sequence length, every single time
Generating a 1,000-token response would mean redoing huge chunks of the same math roughly 1,000 times over

slides.title: Cache the Keys and Values, Reuse Them
slides.body: Self-attention needs three projections per token: Query, Key, and Value. A token's Key and Value vectors never change once computed — so the model stores them in a KV cache and reuses them at every future step.
bullets: Only the new token's Query needs to attend against all the already-cached Keys and Values
Turns per-step attention cost from full recomputation over the sequence into one new-token computation plus a cache lookup

slides.title: What's Actually Stored
slides.body: The cache holds one Key vector and one Value vector per token, per attention head, per layer — and it grows with every token generated.
bullets: Cache size scales with: layers × heads × head-dimension × sequence length × batch size
For a multi-billion-parameter model serving long contexts, this cache alone can occupy several gigabytes of GPU memory per active conversation

slides.title: Techniques That Shrink the Cache
slides.body: Because the KV cache is often the actual memory bottleneck during long-context serving — not the model weights — several techniques exist specifically to shrink or manage it.

rows: Fewer KV heads than Query heads
Bytes stored per value (e.g. FP16 → INT8)

slides.title: A Concrete Bottleneck
slides.body: Take a mid-size model serving several concurrent users, each holding a long multi-turn conversation. Without any cache-shrinking tricks, the combined KV cache can require far more GPU memory than the model's own weights.
bullets: This is why 'context length' and 'concurrent users' — not just model size — are often the real limits on serving cost
It's also part of why providers charge more, or throttle, for very long conversation histories

slides.title: When the Cache Becomes the Bottleneck
bullets: Long context plus high concurrency: cache memory can exceed available GPU VRAM before compute even becomes the limit
Naive allocation wastes memory to fragmentation — exactly what PagedAttention (used in vLLM) fixes, by managing the cache in fixed-size pages the way an OS manages RAM
Streaming very long documents without cache management can silently degrade a serving system well before it fails with a clean error

slides.title: The Cache Is Why Chat Feels Fast — and Isn't Free
bullets: KV caching turns per-token attention from full recomputation into incremental lookup — the single biggest reason autoregressive decoding is usable at all
Cache size grows with context length, batch size, layers, and heads — it's often the real memory bottleneck in serving, not the weights
GQA, quantization, and PagedAttention are three independent, stackable ways to shrink or manage that cost

questions.prompt: What does the KV cache actually store?
options: The model's weights, compressed
Each token's Key and Value vectors, per layer and per attention head
A copy of the raw input prompt text
The final output logits for reuse
questions.explanation: Once a token's Key and Value projections are computed they don't change, so caching them per layer and per attention head avoids recomputing them on every subsequent decoding step.

questions.prompt: Why does the KV cache grow the way it does during generation?
options: It shrinks as generation continues
It grows with sequence length, batch size, and the model's layer/head count, multiplicatively
It only depends on model size, not context length
It's a fixed size set once at model load time
questions.explanation: Cache size scales with how many tokens have been generated (sequence length), how many requests are served at once (batch size), and the model's own layer and head counts — all multiplied together.

questions.prompt: What problem does PagedAttention (used in vLLM) specifically address?
options: Reducing the number of attention heads in the model
Making the model more accurate on benchmarks
Managing KV cache memory allocation to avoid fragmentation and waste
Compressing model weights down to INT8
questions.explanation: PagedAttention manages the KV cache in fixed-size pages, similar to how an operating system manages physical memory, so memory isn't wasted on fragmentation or over-allocated for a worst-case sequence length.

posts.title: Claude Formalizes Fermat's Last Theorem in Lean
posts.subtitle: 11 days, 13 million lines of Lean, and 30,300 verified theorems.
posts.summary: Anthropic used teams of Claude agents to produce the first complete, machine-checked Lean formalization of Fermat's Last Theorem, coordinated through a DAG-structured platform called Prove2Me. The math wasn't new (Wiles proved it in 1995) — the achievement is verifying a proof of this scale the way you'd verify a calculation.

slides.title: 350 Years, 11 Days
slides.body: Andrew Wiles proved Fermat's Last Theorem in 1995 after 350+ years of failed attempts. Anthropic just had Claude produce the first complete, computer-verified formalization of that proof in the Lean proof language.

slides.title: A Lean Proof Is a Different Beast Than a Paper Proof
slides.body: A proof a mathematician finds persuasive on paper is not the same as a proof a computer can check line-by-line with zero ambiguity.
bullets: Wiles's proof spans deep number theory: modularity, elliptic curves, Galois representations
Formalizing existing big theorems into Lean is notoriously slow — often years of work per theorem
No one had produced a full Lean formalization of FLT before this project

slides.title: Prove2Me: A Dependency Graph Agents Could Split Across
slides.body: The project ran on Prove2Me, an open collaborative platform that tracks every theorem as a node in a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of dependencies.
bullets: Multiple Claude agents (roughly Fable-5.1-level) worked in parallel through a code-based multi-agent harness
Theorem statements were separated from their proofs, so agents could cite results before they were finished
The DAG structure avoided the memory degradation that hits single long-running agents on huge tasks

slides.title: The Scale of It
slides.body: These aren't estimates — they're what the project actually consumed, and the finished proof is bigger than the community's entire shared math library.

rows: 5x larger than the whole community proof library

slides.title: A Smaller Test Ran on Consumer Subscriptions
slides.body: Separately, three people formalized Vinogradov's Three Primes Theorem through Prove2Me using ordinary consumer Claude Max subscriptions — not a special research harness — in just 3 days.
bullets: Same Prove2Me DAG approach, far smaller team
Consumer-tier Claude subscriptions, not an internal research model
3 days for a smaller but still real analytic number theory result

slides.title: The Proof Works. It's Not Pretty.
slides.body: The team was explicit about the rough edges.
bullets: About 7% of early non-boilerplate lines came from failed attempts before Prove2Me existed
The finished proof is 'likely much longer than it needs to be' vs. hand-written Mathlib style
It took ~6 billion tokens — a real cost, not a cheap trick
Humans still gave occasional high-level direction; it wasn't fully autonomous

slides.title: What This Actually Proves
slides.body: The novelty isn't new mathematics — it's verification at scale. Mathematician Kevin Buzzard called it 'a big step towards automatic formalization of the modern mathematical literature.'
bullets: Formal verification at this scale used to be reserved for small, cherished results
The bottleneck shifts from 'can an AI find the proof' to 'can the infrastructure keep tens of thousands of theorems consistent'
Expect DAG-structured multi-agent verification to spread to any domain where agents build large, checkable artifacts

A disproof of a special case of FLT
A simplified elementary proof requiring no elliptic curves
questions.explanation: The math wasn't new — Wiles proved FLT in 1995. What's new is a complete, computer-verified Lean formalization of a simplified version of that proof, which is a verification achievement, not a mathematical one.

questions.prompt: What problem did the Prove2Me DAG structure solve?
options: It let multiple agents work on independent theorem branches in parallel without redoing each other's work
It compressed the final proof to be shorter than Mathlib
It reduced the tokens needed to zero
It replaced Lean with a faster proof language
questions.explanation: By tracking dependencies as a DAG and separating theorem statements from proofs, agents could reference not-yet-finished results and split work across the tree instead of colliding on the same subgoals.

options: The proof cannot be checked by anyone outside Anthropic

It only works for Fermat's Last Theorem and no other theorem
Claude wrote the proof with zero human involvement at any point
questions.explanation: The team noted the proof is probably longer than necessary compared to hand-crafted Mathlib style, and getting there took roughly 6 billion output tokens plus occasional human high-level steering.

posts.title: Claude Rewrote AlphaFold's GPU Kernels, 4x Faster
posts.subtitle: One kernel got 2.9x faster, and a full ribosome now fits on one GPU node.
posts.summary: Anthropic set Claude loose on 30+ open-source biomolecular models (AlphaFold3, OpenFold3, Boltz-2, and others) for about four weeks with minimal supervision. The result: roughly 4x average speedup, custom GPU kernels 2-3x faster than the prior standard, and single-GPU predictions of structures over 10,000 tokens like the human mitochondrial Complex I and the 70S ribosome.

slides.title: Four Weeks, Minimal Supervision, 4x Speedup
slides.body: Anthropic pointed Claude at 30+ open-source biomolecular models — structure prediction, protein design, genomics, protein language models — and let it optimize them.
bullets: Models included AlphaFold3, OpenFold3, and Boltz-2
Result: roughly 4x average acceleration, about 2x with bit-identical outputs

slides.title: The Bottleneck Isn't the Model, It's the Kernel
slides.body: These models spend most of their compute inside 'triangle attention' and 'triangle multiplication' — the geometric core of AlphaFold-style architectures.
bullets: Hand-written GPU kernels for these ops hadn't been revisited in years, even as H100/H200/B300 GPUs shipped
Without faster kernels, systems bigger than a single protein (a full complex, a ribosome) simply don't fit computationally

slides.title: FlashPairformer: New Kernels for a Decade-Old Bottleneck

bullets: 2.7-2.9x faster than the prior industry-standard kernel on triangle attention
1.7-3.2x faster on triangle multiplication
A new 'Big' mode lets a single GPU node predict systems over 10,000 tokens

slides.title: A Repeatable Playbook, Not a One-Off
bullets: An AI agent iteratively rewriting low-level GPU kernels for an existing scientific model is a pattern, not a one-time trick
Real, measurable systems wins (2-4x) can come from weeks of agentic kernel engineering rather than new research
Whole-genome-scale structure prediction on a single GPU node is now realistic for labs without supercomputer budgets
