posts.title: Function Calling: Teaching LLMs to Use Tools
posts.subtitle: How a model goes from generating text to actually doing things
posts.summary: Function calling lets an LLM emit a structured, schema-constrained request instead of prose when a task needs real data or a real action — the calling application executes it and feeds the result back, grounding the model's next response in reality.

slides.title: Function Calling: Teaching LLMs to Use Tools
slides.body: An LLM is a text predictor — it can't check today's weather, query a database, or send an email on its own. Function calling is the mechanism that lets it ask for those things in a form software can act on.

slides.title: Text prediction alone can't touch the real world
slides.body: Ask a plain LLM for tomorrow's weather and it will confidently guess — because guessing plausible text is all it knows how to do. It has no way to actually query anything.
bullets: No built-in way to fetch live data, run code, or change external state
Left unconstrained, it hallucinates a plausible-sounding answer instead
The fix isn't a smarter model — it's a structured channel to real actions

slides.title: The mechanism: schema in, structured call out
slides.body: Each tool is described to the model as a JSON Schema — a name, a description, and typed parameters. When the model decides a tool fits, it emits a structured call instead of freeform prose.
bullets: Developer defines tools: { name, description, parameters (JSON Schema) }
Schema is injected into the model's context alongside the user's request
Model emits e.g. {"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Paris"}}
Constrained decoding guarantees that output actually parses as valid, schema-matching JSON

slides.title: The loop: call, execute, return, continue
slides.body: Function calling isn't one request — it's a loop between the model and the application running it.
bullets: 1. Model emits a tool call instead of a final answer
2. Application executes the function for real (API call, DB query, code run)
3. Result is appended to the conversation as a new message
4. Model continues — now grounded in real data — and either calls another tool or answers
Some APIs support parallel calls: several tool calls emitted in one turn, executed concurrently

slides.title: Worked example: book a flight, then calendar it
slides.body: User: 'Book me the cheapest flight from SF to NYC next Friday and add it to my calendar.' The model doesn't answer directly — it chains two tool calls.
bullets: Call 1: search_flights(origin='SFO', dest='JFK', date='next Friday', sort='price')
App executes it, returns real flight data (price, times, airline)
Call 2: create_calendar_event(title=..., start=..., end=...) using that flight's actual times
Only after both results return does the model write the natural-language confirmation — grounded in real prices and times, not guesses

slides.title: Native function calling vs. prompted tool use
slides.body: Not every tool-using system relies on model-native function calling — some parse tool calls out of plain generated text (the ReAct pattern).

rows: Model fine-tuned to emit schema-constrained JSON for tool calls
High — invalid JSON is structurally prevented
Model writes 'Action: search(...)' in free text, app regex-parses it
Lower — brittle to formatting drift, needs parsing/retry logic

slides.title: Where it breaks — and when to skip it
slides.body: Function calling adds real failure surface, not just capability.
bullets: Ambiguous tool descriptions cause wrong or malformed arguments ('schema drift')
Too many tools exposed at once measurably hurts selection accuracy — curate, don't dump the whole API surface
Tool outputs are untrusted input to the next model turn — validate/sandbox before executing, never blindly trust a model-issued call
Skip it for single-shot text generation (summarizing, drafting) — the extra loop only adds latency and failure modes with no upside

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Function calling is a structured escape hatch from text-only prediction into real actions
The loop is call → execute → return result → continue, and it can chain across multiple tools
Constrained decoding is what makes the model's tool calls reliably parseable
More tools isn't free — curate the tool list and validate every call before executing it

questions.prompt: Why can't a plain LLM answer 'what's the weather in Paris right now' correctly on its own?
options: It doesn't understand the word 'weather'
It has no built-in way to query live external data — it can only generate plausible-sounding text
Weather questions are too short for it to process
It refuses all questions about real-time data
questions.explanation: An LLM is a text predictor with no inherent connection to live data sources; without a tool to call, it will generate a plausible-sounding but ungrounded guess.

questions.prompt: In the function-calling loop, what happens immediately after the model emits a tool call?
options: The model immediately gives its final answer
The application executes the function and appends the real result back into the conversation
The conversation ends
The user is asked to manually run the function
questions.explanation: The calling application, not the model, executes the function. The real result is appended as a new message so the model's next turn is grounded in actual data.

questions.prompt: What's a known pitfall of exposing too many tools to a model at once?
options: It has no effect on accuracy
It reduces the model's context window permanently
Tool-selection accuracy measurably drops as the number of available tools grows
It makes constrained decoding impossible
questions.explanation: Dumping a large, uncurated tool list into context makes it harder for the model to pick and correctly call the right tool — curation matters as much as capability.

posts.title: GRPO: Reinforcement Learning Without a Critic Network
posts.subtitle: How DeepSeek trained reasoning models by scoring answers against their own group, not a learned value function.
posts.summary: GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) drops PPO's learned critic network, instead scoring each response against a group of sampled peers to compute its advantage. It halves training memory and made large-scale RL for reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1) practical.

slides.body: Standard RLHF trains a critic network the same size as the policy just to estimate how good a response is. GRPO throws it out.
slides.title: PPO needs a second model just to grade the first one
bullets: No value network to train or store
Used to train DeepSeekMath and DeepSeek-R1
Roughly halves GPU memory during RL fine-tuning

slides.body: Proximal Policy Optimization needs a value/critic model — usually initialized from the same base checkpoint as the policy — to predict expected future reward at every token. For a 70B policy, that's another ~70B model to hold in GPU memory and keep numerically stable during training.
slides.title: PPO's critic doubles your memory bill
bullets: Critic must be trained jointly and can itself be unstable or biased
At 70B+ scale, critic weights + optimizer states rival the policy's own footprint
Advantage estimates are only as good as the critic's value predictions

slides.body: For each prompt, GRPO samples a GROUP of G completions (e.g. G=16–64) from the current policy, scores each with a reward function, then uses the group's own mean and standard deviation as the baseline.
slides.title: Replace the critic with a group of siblings
bullets: advantage_i = (reward_i − mean(group rewards)) / std(group rewards)
No learned value function — the baseline comes from sampling, not prediction
KL penalty against a frozen reference model is added directly to the loss, not folded into the reward

slides.body: DeepSeek-R1-Zero trained this way on verifiable domains like math and code.
slides.title: Worked example: one math problem, 64 attempts
bullets: Sample 64 chain-of-thought completions for the same problem from the current policy
Reward is rule-based: 1.0 if the final boxed answer matches the ground truth, else 0.0
A completion that got the right answer only gets positive advantage if it beats the group's average — if 60 of 64 got it right, being right is barely rewarded
No reward model needed at all when correctness is mechanically checkable

slides.title: PPO vs. GRPO

slides.body: Because the baseline is recomputed per-prompt from sampled peers, GRPO never compares rewards across different prompts — only within one prompt's own group.
slides.title: Why 'group-relative' changes what you optimize for
bullets: Absolute reward scale doesn't matter, only rank within the group
Removes the need to normalize rewards across wildly different task difficulties
But it means the signal only exists if the group has variance at all

slides.body: The group-relative trick has real failure modes, not just savings.
slides.title: When GRPO breaks down
bullets: If a prompt is too hard, all G samples fail → identical rewards → zero advantage → zero learning signal
If a prompt is too easy, all G samples succeed → same problem in reverse
Small group sizes (G<8) give a noisy mean/std, producing unstable advantage estimates
Still fully dependent on reward quality — GRPO removes the critic, not the need for a good reward signal

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: GRPO estimates advantage from a sampled group instead of a learned critic — cutting RL memory roughly in half
It shines on verifiable-reward domains (math, code) where correctness is checkable without a reward model
Group size and task difficulty spread directly control how much learning signal you get
It's the RL backbone behind DeepSeekMath and DeepSeek-R1's reasoning gains

questions.prompt: What does GRPO use instead of a learned critic network to estimate advantage?
options: A fixed constant baseline
The mean and standard deviation of rewards within a sampled group of completions
A second, smaller critic trained less frequently
The reward from the previous training step
questions.explanation: GRPO samples G completions per prompt and normalizes each reward against that group's own mean/std — the group itself becomes the baseline, so no separate value network is trained.

questions.prompt: Why can GRPO produce zero learning signal on a very easy or very hard prompt?
options: The KL penalty grows too large
The reward model refuses to score the prompt
If every sampled completion in the group gets the same reward, the group has zero variance so every advantage is zero
GRPO caps the maximum reward per prompt
questions.explanation: Advantage is (reward − group mean) / group std. If all completions succeed or all fail, every reward equals the mean, so every advantage is zero and nothing gets reinforced.

questions.prompt: GRPO is best suited to which kind of task?
options: Open-ended creative writing with no verifiable answer
Tasks with a mechanically checkable reward, like math answers or passing unit tests
Tasks that require a dense, continuously-varying human preference score
Any task, with no dependency on reward quality
questions.explanation: GRPO removes the critic, not the need for a reliable reward. It works best where reward can be computed cheaply and objectively — verifiable math/code correctness is the canonical case, as in DeepSeek-R1-Zero.
